title: Espresso surge profile log — Hemant
content:
Context: small payload, ultra-short-turn interactions ("espresso" = 4–12 token prompts + ~8 token completion). Goal is to understand tail amplification when incoming requests are tiny+fast (client-side batching rare).

Quick goal: capture p50/p95/p99 behavior across three runtime knobs (batching window, kv-cache priming, short-seq kernel path) and a fallback variant (quantized vs full fp16). Want actionable levers to keep p99 under 120ms at 500 qps for tiny requests.

Harness + workload:
- Driver: custom wrk-like harness (local shim) that issues HTTP/1.1 with keepalive, concurrency 200, arrival model poisson with mean inter-arrival tuned to target qps.
- Payload: prompt templates drawn from micro-convo corpus (internal); avg prompt length = 7 tokens, expected completion = 8 tokens.
- Endpoint: /v1/generate (redwood-hosted dev stack) pointing to model: redwood-small-1 (fp16) and redwood-small-1-q4 (quantized).
- Observability: per-request traceid, server-side measure: kernel-path, batch_size_at_infer, kv_cache_hit (bool), model_variant_switched (bool).
- Infra: single A2 instance (1xA100-80GB sim) in dev cluster, background noise: light other tenants (~5% GPU).

Experiment matrix (3x2x2):
- batching_window_ms: 0 (no coalesce), 3ms, 8ms
- kv_cache: cold (fresh container) vs warm (prefilled with 256 primed prefixes)
- variant: fp16 vs q4
- Targets tested: 100 qps, 300 qps, 500 qps

Raw notes from runs (most interesting 300 & 500 qps):
1) 300 qps, batching 0ms, warm cache, fp16:
   - throughput steady ~305 qps (driver), server reported avg batch_size_at_infer ~1.1 (rare coalescing).
   - p50 = 18ms, p95 = 42ms, p99 = 110ms.
   - p99 spikes correlated with GC cycles in python wrapper + small kernel wakeup (see traces).
   - kv_cache_hit ~92% (some misses due to prompt variance).

2) 300 qps, batching 3ms, warm cache, fp16:
   - avg batch_size_at_infer ~1.9.
   - p50 = 22ms (slightly up), p95 = 36ms (slightly down), p99 = 85ms (improved).
   - tail reduction visible: batching absorbed scheduling jitter.

3) 300 qps, batching 8ms, warm cache, fp16:
   - avg batch_size 3.5.
   - p50 = 30ms, p95 = 60ms, p99 = 160ms (worse).
   - explanation: larger batching increases queuing for tiny requests (SLO regression).

4) 500 qps, batching 0ms, warm cache, fp16:
   - server throughput 510 qps. p50 = 22ms, p95 = 58ms, p99 = 220ms (bad).
   - p99 tail formed when small groups of requests collided with kernel warmups and intermittent NVLink stalls (trace sample IDs: 7a2f..).

5) 500 qps, batching 3ms, warm cache, fp16:
   - batch_size 2.1 avg. p50 = 26ms, p95 = 48ms, p99 = 125ms (near target).
   - resource util: GPU util ~78%, kernel occupancy stable.

6) 500 qps, batching 3ms, warm cache, q4 variant:
   - batch_size ~2.0. p50 = 28ms, p95 = 54ms, p99 = 160ms (q4 increased kernel variability).
   - q4 shows single-token generation speed similar but kernel path has rare >50ms wakeups.

7) Cold cache (fresh container), 300 qps, batching 3ms, fp16:
   - kv_cache_hit ~10–12% early; p99 = 420ms. Significant cold-prime penalty.
   - after 90s of steady load, kv_cache_hit climbed to ~85% and p99 moved to ~95ms.

Micro-observations / hypothesis:
- Sweet spot for espresso profiles at these rates appears to be batching_window ≈ 2–4ms. Too small => no jitter absorption; too large => queueing penalty increases latency more than batch benefits.
- KV cache priming dramatically reduces tail during ramp / when containers are recycled. Cold path is killer for p99.
- Quantized variant increases jitter variance (likely kernel selection fallback paths or less mature scheduling). Not worth for tiny requests unless cost pressure is high.
- Python GC and aux threads (tracing, metrics flush) align with many p99 samples. Investigate moving metrics/telemetry to async agent/process or bumping GC thresholds.

Representative ASCII latency histogram (500 qps, batching 3ms, warm cache, fp16):
- p0–p50: 12ms–30ms (dense)
- p50–p95: 30ms–48ms
- p95–p99: 48ms–125ms (long tail)
- >p99.9: rare 220–450ms spikes attributed to cold-priming + kernel wakeups.

Quick command snippets (how I ran):
- driver: ./espresso-harness --url https://dev.redwood/api/generate --concurrency 200 --qps 500 --poisson --keepalive --prompt-corpus micro-espresso.json --traceids out.tsv
- server trace: curl https://dev.redwood/debug/traces?traceid=7a2f.. | jq .

Immediate actions to try (next runs):
- Add micro-window adaptive batching: if avg inter-arrival < 1ms disable batching for that lane; otherwise 3ms. Compare to fixed 3ms.
- Push GC tuning: increase young gen size on python wrapper, move metrics flush to background process.
- Pre-warm KV cache via lightweight priming API on container start (issue steady stream of 12 token prefixes).
- Add jitter to kernel scheduling threads to avoid synchronous wakeup patterns (observed clumping).

Notes for product/ops:
- For low-latency tiny requests we should recommend default batching window 2–4ms and strongly recommend explicit priming during scale-ups and container restarts.
- Quantized variants are good for cost but have tail jitter caveats for tiny requests — flag as "best for bulk/medium-length workloads."

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are the NVLink stalls reproducible on a dedicated/slightly noisier instance? Need a run on isolated A100 dedicated instance.
- What's the right heuristic to decide when to coalesce vs pass-through on a per-tenant basis?
- Are any hardware counters (SM stalls, PCIe latency) correlated with the q4 tails?

TL;DR (for my future self): keep batching short (3ms) for espresso profiles, always warm KV before traffic, avoid q4 for sub-20-token requests unless cost needs justify it, and fix GC/telemetry noise.

-- Hemant

Notes-to-self: attach traces to JIRA-RT-4053, schedule isolated-run with SRE next week, and demo the micro-window policy in the next perf-sprint sync.
